subtopic: Trends in Atomic and Physical Properties
stem: Atomic numbers of the group 13 elements are in the order B < Al < Ga < In < Tl. Arrange these elements in increasing order of ionic radii of \(\mathrm{M^{3\oplus}}\).
solution:
The given elements are in an increasing order of atomic number. As we go down the group 13, their general outer electronic configuration is \(n\mathrm{s}^2 n\mathrm{p}^1\). \(\mathrm{M^{3\oplus}}\) is formed by removal of three electrons from the outermost shell 'n'. In the \(\mathrm{M^{3\oplus}}\) the 'n-1' shell becomes the outermost. Size of the added 'n-1' shell increases down the group. Therefore the ionic radii of \(\mathrm{M^{3\oplus}}\) also increase down the group as follows :

\(\mathrm{B^{3\oplus} < Al^{3\oplus} < Ga^{3\oplus} < In^{3\oplus} < Tl^{3\oplus}}\)
_note: p-00, printed p.123. Labelled `Problem 9.1 :` with its own `Solution :`.

subtopic: Trends in Atomic and Physical Properties
stem: Why the atomic radius of Gallium is less than that of aluminium ?
solution: Atomic radius increases down the group due to added new shell. 'Al' does not have 'd' electrons. As we go from Al down to 'Ga' the nuclear charge increase by 18 units. Out of the 18 electrons added, 10 electrons are in the inner 3d subshell. 'd' Electrons offer poor shielding effect. Therefore, the effects of attraction due to increased nuclear charge is experienced prominently by the outer electrons of 'Ga' and thus its atomic radius becomes smaller than that of 'Al'.
_note: p-01 left column, printed p.124. ⚠ THE BOOK LABELS THIS `Problems 9.2` — PLURAL, and with NO colon after the number, unlike every other worked example in the chapter (`Problem 9.1 :`, `Problem 9.3 :`). That is why a scan for `Problem 9.<n>` reports 9.2 as missing. Verified on the rendered page: the worked example EXISTS and the book skips nothing.

subtopic: Trends in Atomic and Physical Properties
stem: The values of the first ionization enthalpy of Al, Si and P are 577, 786 and 1012 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) respectively. Explain the observed trend.
solution: The trend shows increasing first ionization enthalpy from Al to Si to P. Al, Si and P belong to 13 period in the periodic table. They have same valence shell. Due to the increased nuclear charge electrons in the valence shell are more tightly held by the nucleus as we go from Al to Si to P. Therefore more energy is required to remove an electron from its outermost shell.
_note: p-01, printed p.124, full-width box. ⚠ The printed solution says Al, Si and P 'belong to 13 period' — they are period-3 elements of groups 13, 14 and 15. Preserved as printed and bracketed in errata; the conclusion (same valence shell, rising nuclear charge) does not depend on it.

stem: Why \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 1}}\) ion is more stable than \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 3}}\) ?
solution: Tl is a heavy element which belongs to group 13 of the p-block. The common oxidation state for this group is 3. In p-block, the lower oxidation state is more stable for heavier elements due to inert pair effect. Therefore, \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 1}}\) ion is more stable than \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 3}}\) ion.
_note: p-02, printed p.125. The book writes the charge as a circled plus FOLLOWED by the number (Tl⊕1, Tl⊕3); transcribed faithfully as \oplus.

stem: \(\mathrm{GeCl_4}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{GeCl_2}\) while \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\). Explain.
solution: Ge and Pb are the 4\(^{\text{th}}\) and 5\(^{\text{th}}\) period elements down the group 14. The group oxidation state of group 14 is 4 and the stability of other oxidation state, lower by 2 units, increases down the group due to inert pair effect. The stability of the oxidation state 2 is more in Pb than in Ge.
_note: p-04 left column, printed p.127. In the text layer this example appears AFTER 9.6 because of the two-column flow; on the page 9.5 is the upper-left box and 9.6 the lower-left box.

stem: Nitrogen does not form \(\mathrm{NCl_5}\) or \(\mathrm{NF_5}\) but phosphorous can. Explain.
solution: Phosphorous and other members of the group can make use of d-orbitals in their bonding and thus compounds \(\mathrm{MX_3}\), as well \(\mathrm{MX_5}\) are formed. Nitrogen can not form \(\mathrm{NCl_5}\) or \(\mathrm{NF_5}\) since it is void of d-orbitals in its second shell.
